Introduction

[
1
]

Following are my reasons in respect of a number
of applications brought in the two proceedings. The proceedings arise from a
dispute between the parties after the termination of a lease between Delane
Industry Co. Ltd. (“Delane”) and Tsawassen Quay Market Corporation (“TQMC”),
the previous landlord.

[
2
]

The dispute stretches back over a decade when TQMC,
the landlord, declined to renew Delane’s sublease made March 14, 2005 and
amended March 31, 2006 (the “Sublease”) of a retail space located in the public
market at the British Columbia ferry terminal in Tsawwassen, British Columbia
(the “Tsawwassen Market”). In April 2010,
TQMC
brought
a petition seeking a declaration that Delane had failed to exercise its
contractual right to renew the Sublease.
In May 2010,
Delane commenced an action seeking a declaration that it had validly exercised
its right to renew the Sublease (the “Main Action”).
The petition and
action were heard together before Justice Griffin, as she then was, in January
and February 2011.

[
3
]

In reasons released February 15, 2011, indexed
as
Tsawwassen Quay Market Corporation v. Delane Industry Co. Ltd.
,

2011
BCSC 310
, Justice Griffin determined that Delane had not validly exercised its
right to renew the Sublease, and dismissed this portion of Delane’s claim. A
remaining issue, being the proper amounts to be charged to Delane for common
area expenses under the Sublease, had previously been referred to a registrar
pursuant to the order of Justice Gerow made at a case management conference on
November 16, 2010. The only recent, substantive step taken in the reference to
the registrar occurred on September 21, 2021 when Registrar Nielson, as he then
was, ordered that TQMC produce a number of documents concerning common area
expenses for the Tsawwassen Market (the “Document Production Order”).

[
4
]

Following the issuance of Justice Griffin’s
reasons, in June 2012, Karry Au Yeung, the owner of Delane, published
complaints alleging nefarious conduct by TQMC, its CEO Gary Mathiesen and CFO
Andrew Sam. It is disputed whether Mr. Au Yeung did so in his personal
capacity or in his capacity as a representative of Delane.

[
5
]

In February 2014, TQMC, Mr. Mathiesen and
Mr. Sam commenced a defamation action (the “Defamation Action”) against
Delane and Mr. Au Yeung which resulted in a settlement agreement (the
“Settlement Agreement”).

Under
the Settlement Agreement, Mr. Au Yeung and Delane agreed to cease defaming
TQMC, Mr. Mathiesen and Mr. Sam in exchange for their agreement to discontinue
the Defamation Action.
The Settlement Agreement resulted
in the issuance of a consent order by Justice Harris, as she then was, on March
17, 2017, prohibiting such conduct (the “Defamation Order”).

Orders Sought

[
6
]

Although a total of six related applications in
both the Main Action and the Defamation Action were filed and set to be heard
during the week of July 11, 2022, only four applications proceeded.

[
7
]

First, in its application filed September 27,
2021 in the Main Action, TQMC applies for a stay of proceedings until Mr. Au
Yeung and Delane have purged their contempt for breach of the Defamation Order.
TQMC also seeks special costs of this application. At the hearing before me, TQMC
abandoned its application for an order that Mr. Au Yeung be committed or
fined for breach of the Document Production Order by breaching the implied
undertaking rule by improperly disclosing various documents provided by TQMC. I
will refer to this application as Application No. 1.

[
8
]

Second, pursuant to its application filed
September 27, 2021 in the Defamation Action, TQMC, Mr. Mathiesen and Mr. Sam
apply for an order that Mr. Au Yeung and Delane each be fined for
breaching the Defamation Order by publishing defamatory statements between May
28 and July 29, 2021. The applicants seek fines against both Mr. Au Yeung
and Delane of $5,000 payable to the Province of British Columbia and special
costs of this application. I will refer to this application as Application No.
2.

[
9
]

Third, in its application filed November 10,
2021 in the Main Action, Delane seeks an order that TQMC, Mr. Mathiesen
and Mr. Sam be found in contempt and fined for failing to comply with the
Document Production Order.
The applicants seek fines against
TQMC of $1,000 per week until it has purged its contempt, lump-sum fines of $50,000
against TQMC and $5,000 against each of Mr. Mathiesen, TQMC’s president
Taylor Mathiesen and Mr. Sam, and weekly fines against these individuals
of $1,000 until they have purged their contempt. Delane also seeks special
costs of this application. I
will refer to this application as Application
No. 3.

[
10
]

Fourth, in its application filed June 20, 2022 in the Main Action, TQMC
seeks an order that Delane pay security for costs of this proceeding in the amount
of $15,000, failing which the Main Action should be stayed. I will refer to
this application as Application No. 4.

[
11
]

At the hearing before me, Delane abandoned or
adjourned generally the relief sought in its application filed February 3, 2022
in the Main Action seeking to, amongst other things, strike out the September
27, 2021 applications
brought by TQMC, Mr. Mathiesen
and Mr. Sam.
In addition, Delane abandoned its
application filed April 13, 2022 in the Main Action seeking various orders
including payment of overcharged rent, production of documents and declarations
that Mr. Mathiesen filed a false affidavit and similar orders related to
alleged fraud or contempt of court.

Application No. 1

[
12
]

Mr. Au Yeung and Delane submit, and I find, that the TQMC
application for a stay of the Main Action is fundamentally flawed after TQMC
abandoned its applications for contempt of the Document Production Order, and
therefore must be dismissed.

[
13
]

At Part 1, para. 1 of the notice of application filed September
27, 2021 in the Main Action, TQMC sought an order that Mr. Au Yeung be
committed, fined or both, and that Delane be fined for contempt of the Document
Production Order by breaching the implied undertaking of confidentiality with
respect to documents produced by TQMC pursuant to this order. As well, TQMC
sought an order for contempt against Mr. Au Yeung and Delane for
publishing defamatory statements regarding TQMC and Mr. Mathiesen. As I
noted earlier in my reasons, at the hearing before me on July 11, 2022, TQMC
abandoned the relief sought at para. 1 of its notice of application.

[
14
]

At Part 1, para. 2 of its notice of
application, TQMC seeks an order that:

[t]he
proceedings
in this action
and all other proceedings
in this action

be stayed until such date that [Mr. Au Yeung and Delane] obtain an order
of this court declaring that they have purged their contempt for
the Order

and their contempt of this court. (emphasis added).

[
15
]

The “Order” is defined to be the order of Registrar Nielsen. Given
that TQMC has abandoned its application seeking a finding that Mr. Au
Yeung or Delane have breached this order, there is no contempt of this order to
purge and therefore no basis to grant a stay. The Defamation Order of Justice Harris
was made in a different action and contempt of this order cannot be used to
justify a finding of contempt in respect of the order of Registrar Nielsen, an
entirely different order in a different proceeding.

[
16
]

Application No. 1 of TQMC is dismissed with one set of costs awarded
to the respondents Delane and Mr. Au Yeung.

Application No. 2

[
17
]

As stated earlier in these reasons, the dispute between Mr. Au
Yeung and Delane on the one side, and TQMC and its management on the other,
arises from the termination of the Sublease at the Tsawwassen Market over 10 years
ago. Clearly Mr. Au Yeung has considered for some time that he has been
wronged.

[
18
]

On June 13, 2012, Mr. Au Yeung sent a
letter to then Premier Christy Clark, then CEO of BC Ferries Mike Corrigan, and
others stating as follows:

I confirm that Gary Mathiesen is a liar, a
cheater and a professional crook after the last law suit. Accounting record is
there. If he said he is not a lier, not a cheater, and not a professional
crook, [a]sk him to follow court orders to give out accounting detail and prove
himself to be a good person and prove his team is good management company.

Gary Mathiesen
and his team are not only cheating Delane Canada. They are cheating all their
sub-tenants and B.C. ferries …

[
19
]

As set out above, in 2014, the parties entered
into the Settlement Agreement under which Mr. Au Yeung and Delane agreed
not to further defame TQMC, Mr. Mathiesen and Mr. Sam. The subsequently
issued Defamation Order is as follows:

1.         By
consent, it is declared that the Plaintiffs Gary Mathiesen, Andrew Sam and
Tsawwassen Quay Market Corporation and the Defendants Karry Au Yeung and Delane
Industry Co. Ltd. entered into and made a binding and enforceable contract to
settle all the issues in this action S-125760 through a settlement offer made
by the Plaintiffs on February 24, 2014 and accepted by the Defendants on
February 25, 2014 (the “Settlement Agreement”);

2.         By
consent, it is declared that the terms of the Settlement Agreement are as
follows:

(a) the Defendants and each of them are hereby restrained
and prohibited from defaming the Plaintiffs and each of them in any way,
anywhere and by any means, be it publication of libel by any means or slander;

…

3.         The Defendants and each them
are hereby restrained and prohibited from defaming the Plaintiffs and each of
them in any way, anywhere and by any means, be it by publication of libel by any
means, or by slander.

[
20
]

On July 29, 2021, Mr. Au Yeung sent an
email (the “July 2021 Email”) to the new CEO of BC Ferries, Mike Collins, the
British Columbia Minster of Transport, the Attorney General of British Columbia
and various subtenants of TQMC at the Tsawwassen Market. In his email Mr. Au
Yeung made comments including the following:

Yes I had repeatedly call Mr. Gary Mathiesen
a LIAR, CHEATER, CROOK AND PROFESSIONAL CROOK because he had planed everything
to lie and cheat me and trick me and all the subtenants …

More than 10
years ago, Mr. Mathiesen and/or his consul had mislead the judge to
transfer the case to the registrar so Mr. Mathieson and TQMC will not be sued
for lying and cheating.

[
21
]

Mr. Au Yeung had attached to the July 2021
Email an email dated May 27, 2021 which had been sent to the same parties. In his
May 27, 2021 email, he made comments including the following:

Mr. Mathiesen had totally intentionally
over charged all of completely …

… This was a total intentional and it was a
total FRAUD to overcharge or cheat me and all of you.

I had been calling Mr. Mathiesen (a Charter
Accountant and managing CEO of TQMC) and his certified management accountant
Mr. Andrew Sam, liars, cheaters, crooks and professional crooks, since I got
the first TQMC common area expenses statement around middle of 2006 …

...

… Mr. Mathiesen
had been intentionally charged us all untrue expenses. Mr. Mathiesen and TQMC
had been intentionally lying and cheating us and you for all these untrue
expenses. Mr. Mathiesen and TQMC had been intentionally lying and cheating us
and you for all these untrue expenses. Mr. Mathiesen and Mr. Sam had planned
everything to overcharged us and all their subtenants in Tsawwssen Quay Market.
This is  a commercial crime and not a commercial argument.

[
22
]

The applicants contend that Mr. Au Yeung’s July 2021 Email attaching
the email dated May 27, 2021 was defamatory, and sending the email constitutes
an intentional breach of the Defamation Order justifying a finding of contempt
and the imposition of the fines sought against both Mr. Au Yeung and
Delane.

[
23
]

In the application response filed October 22,
2021 on behalf of both Mr. Au Yeung and Delane, the respondents take the
position that the comments set out in Mr. Au Yeung’s emails concerning Mr. Mathiesen
and Mr. Sam are true and therefore not defamatory.
At the hearing before me, Mr. Au Yeung represented himself and
Delane was separately represented by counsel.

[
24
]

In oral submissions, Mr. Au Yeung continued to take the
position that the comments in his emails were true and therefore not defamatory.
He submitted that if his comments were defamatory, he should be given an
opportunity to purge his contempt – although he did not explain how he would do
so. After being taken to caselaw provided by TQMC indicating that truthfulness
is not a defence, counsel for Delane effectively conceded that this caselaw
(which I will discuss below) indicated that even if the comments made by Mr. Au
Yeung in his emails were true they could still be found to be defamatory.

Analysis – Defamatory Conduct

[
25
]

In this application, the first issue to be decided is whether the
comments in Mr. Au Yeung’s July 2021 Email were defamatory. The next
question is whether the defences of justification or truth apply in this case.

Were the Comments Defamatory?

[
26
]

A defamatory statement is one which, in the eyes of a reasonable
person, lowers the reputation of a person about whom they are made:
R. v.
Dhillon
,

2019 BCCA 373
at para.
43
[
Dhillon CA
],
referring to the decision in
Taseko Mines Limited v. Western Canada
Wilderness Committee
,

2017 BCCA 431
at paras.
41-45
.

[
27
]

Allegations of dishonourable or dishonest conduct made against an
individual acting in a professional capacity will typically meet the definition
of defamation:
Dhillon CA
at para.
43
, referring to the decision in
Weaver
v. Corcoran
,

2017 BCCA 160
at para
68
.

[
28
]

Stating that someone has lied in the course of their business is
defamatory:
Pan v. Gao
,

2020 BCCA 58
at paras.
100-103
.

[
29
]

I have little difficulty concluding that the comments in Mr. Au
Yeung’s emails are defamatory. Use of the words “liar”, “cheater” and “crook”
to describe Mr. Mathiesen and Mr. Sam, essentially accusing them of theft,
in the context of their role as officers of TQMC would clearly lower their
reputation in the eyes of a reasonable person. These are not the only examples
of defamatory comments set out in Mr. Au Yeung’s emails.

Does the Defence of Justification or
Truth Apply?

[
30
]

Whether or not a statement is justified or true does not prevent it
from being found to be defamatory if it lowers the reputation of an individual.
As set out in a leading text on defamation,
Brown on Defamation
, “[t]he
law presumes in favour of the plaintiff that the defamatory words are false.
Once the statements are made or published that lower the reputation of the
plaintiff, a defamation exists whether or not the statements are true. The
elements of falsity is only a legal presumption which arises after the
defamation already exists”: Raymond E. Brown,
Brown on Defamation:
Canada,
United Kingdom, Australia, New Zealand, United States, 2nd ed., loose-leaf
(updated 2013), (Toronto: Carswell, 1994), vol. 3 ch. 10 at 10-7,
referred to in
R. v. Dhillon
,

2014 BCSC
1986

at para.
18
[
Dhillon

BCSC
].

[
31
]

The British Columbia Court of Appeal upheld the
findings of Justice Holmes, as she then was, in
Dhillon CA

that the
character of a statement determines whether it is defamatory, not whether the
statement is false. At para. 42 of
Dhillon CA
, the Court of Appeal found
no error in the following conclusion made by Justice Holmes in
Dhillon

BCSC

at para. 19, that truth or justification is a defence to an action in tort, but
does not negate whether the statement itself is defamatory:

[
19]      In this sense, according to the law that
applies to the tort of defamation, statements may be defamatory even though
they are justified or true. Justification or truth provides the defendant with
a defence to the action in tort, but does not change the statements’ defamatory
character if, at the first stage, they are shown to be statements which
reasonable or right-thinking members of society would understand as lowering
the reputation of the person about whom they are made.

[
32
]

In this case, as is confirmed by reasoning of the Court of Appeal in

Dhillon CA
at para.
44
, whether or not the comments made by Mr. Au
Yeung are true or justified, or Mr. Au Yeung believed them to be so, is
irrelevant. The relevant question is whether a right-thinking member of society
would understand the comments to lower the reputation of the party about whom
they were made:
Dhillon CA

at para.
43
.

Analysis – Contempt

[
33
]

The final issue is whether, by making the defamatory comments in the
July 2021 Email, Mr. Au Yeung and Delane should be found in contempt of court
for breaching the Defamation Order.

[
34
]

The three elements that must be proven beyond a reasonable doubt to
establish civil contempt include the following: first, the order must state
clearly and unequivocally what should or should not be done; second, the party
alleged to have breached the order must have actual knowledge of the order; and
finally, the party that is alleged to have breached the order must have
intentionally done the act that the order prohibited:
Wei v. Chiu
,

2019
BCSC 441
at para.
28
, referring to,
inter alia
,
Carey v. Laiken
,

2015 SCC 17
at paras.
32-35
.

[
35
]

I am satisfied that the applicants have proven the elements required
for a finding of civil contempt, beyond a reasonable doubt.

[
36
]

First, the Defamation Order prohibited Mr. Au
Yeung and Delane from defaming TQMC, Mr. Mathiesen and Mr. Sam “in
any way, anywhere and by any means”. I have little difficulty concluding that
this prohibition was clear and unequivocal.

[
37
]

Second, there is no doubt that Mr. Au Yeung and Delane, as
parties to the Settlement Agreement which preceded the Defamation Order itself –
which I again note went by consent, had knowledge of this order. Relevant
evidence includes the following:

a)

The Defamation Order was signed by then legal counsel for Mr. Au
Yeung and Delane;

b)

Mr. Au Yeung and Delane, on their own and without counsel,
applied to vary the Defamation Order on October 30, 2020; and

c)

Mr. Au Yeung specifically stated in the July 2021 Email that
“[t]here is an injunction order that I will not defame Mr. Mathiesen.”

[
38
]

Third, there is no doubt that Mr. Au Yeung intentionally sent
the July 2021 Email and attached his earlier email of May 27, 2021. The emails
both bear Mr. Au Yeung’s name on the signature line and the emails
originate from the same email address. Mr. Au Yeung has sworn affidavits
in these proceedings deposing to have sent emails from this email account. As
well, Mr. Au Yeung and Delane have filed a notice of intention to act in person
showing this email address as their address for service. The content of the
emails, being allegations of misconduct by Mr. Mathieson and Mr. Sam,
directed to government officials and other subtenants at Tsawwassen Market, also
make it clear that the emails were sent intentionally.

[
39
]

There is no doubt that the emails sent by Mr. Au Yeung defamed
Mr. Mathieson and Mr. Sam in that Mr. Au Yeung identifies one or
both of them as “liars, cheaters, crooks and professional crooks” in carrying
out their role administering the subleases at Tsawwassen Market.

[
40
]

In summary, I find that the Defamation Order clearly states that Mr. Au
Yeung and Delane are prohibited from defaming the applicants, that Mr. Au
Yeung, the owner of Delane, had knowledge of this order and intentionally
defamed the applicants by sending the July 2021 Email. Accordingly, a finding
of contempt is justified.

[
41
]

The applicants submit that both Mr. Au
Yeung and Delane should be found in contempt and fined. The Defamation Order
prohibited both Mr. Au Yeung and Delane collectively and individually from
defaming the applicants. I find that both are guilty of civil of contempt, Mr. Au
Yeung in his personal capacity and Delane vicariously.

Appropriate Sanction for Contempt

[
42
]

Rule 22-8(1) of the
Supreme Court Civil Rules
, B.C.
Reg. 168/2009, provides that this Court may punish contempt by an order
for committal or a fine or both. As I have already stated, the applicants do
not seek committal but rather a fine.

[
43
]

One purpose for sentencing in civil contempt is to punish the
contemnor for breaching a court order. As stated in
Carey
, at para.
31
,
“Courts sometimes impose a substantial fine to match the gravity of the
contempt, to deter the contemnor’s continuing conduct and to deter others from
similar conduct”.

[
44
]

In
College of Physicians and Surgeons of British Columbia v.
Ezzati
,

2021 BCCA 422
at paras.
56-59 and 64
, Justice Fitch set out examples
of factors which the court may consider in determining an appropriate sanction.
These factors include the following:

a)

The sentence should be proportionate to the gravity of the conduct
and the degree of responsibility of the contemnor (para. 56);

b)

The sentencing objectives of general and specific deterrence, and
denunciation are to be considered (para. 57);

c)

Similar sentences should be imposed for similarly-situated
contemnors (at para. 58);

d)

Judicial restraint should be exercised in considering committal for
civil contempt, and other sanctions should be considered first – especially for
a first breach (para. 59); and

e)

Other factors such as past conduct, whether the contemnor has
profited by their contempt or whether the contemnor has apologized for their
conduct may be considered (para. 64).

[
45
]

The applicants submit that a fine of $5,000 payable by each of Mr. Au
Yeung and Delane is appropriate, in light of the gravity of their intentional
breach of the Defamation Order and their past history of defaming the
applicants, to deter them from similar conduct in the future, and because they
have not apologized or shown any remorse for their conduct. The applicants have
not directed the court to any authorities where a similar fine has been ordered.

[
46
]

In my view, the gravity of the offence is significant. The July 2021
defamatory conduct at issue in this application is virtually identical to that
which occurred when Mr. Au Yeung first published defamatory statements
about Mr. Mathiesen and Mr. Sam in 2013.
Despite
consenting to the terms of the Defamation Order, Mr. Au Yeung repeated his
very serious allegations of financial misconduct against Mr. Mathiesen and
Mr. Sam, both professional accountants
. I consider that Mr. Au Yeung
did this intending to harm the professional reputation of Mr. Mathiesen
and Mr. Sam, and the business of TQMC.

[
47
]

When he sent the July 2021 Email, Mr. Au Yeung was acting not
simply in his personal capacity but also in his capacity as the owner of Delane.
In my view, this justifies the imposition of a significant financial penalty to
deter both Mr. Au Yeung and others from this type of undesirable conduct
in the commercial context.

[
48
]

As the applicants point out Mr. Au Yeung has not backed down
from his allegations of misconduct by issuing a retraction or seeking to
apologize.

[
49
]

I find that in the circumstances, a fine of $5,000 payable by each
of Mr. Au Yeung and Delane to the Province of British Columbia is
appropriate.

Costs of this Application

[
50
]

The
applicants seek special costs of this application. Special costs are awarded to
punish and deter reprehensible conduct in the course of a litigation:
Smithies
Holdings Inc. v. RCV Holdings Ltd.
,

2017 BCCA 177
at para.
134
.

[
51
]

With respect to costs, I consider that Mr. Au Yeung’s conduct
is reprehensible in that it suggest that he never intended to comply with the
Defamation Order but rather considered, wrongly, that despite consenting to
this order, he could say what he wanted about Mr. Mathiesen and Mr. Sam,
so long as he could prove that his allegations were true.

[
52
]

In this case, the applicants, who compromised their defamation claim
when they agreed to the Defamation Order, should not be required to incur
expense in assisting the Court with enforcing the Defamation Order:
North
Vancouver (District) v. Sorrenti
,
2004 BCCA 316
at para.
20
. I order
that costs of this application be payable to the applicants on a special costs
basis.

Application No. 3

[
53
]

As set out above, Delane seeks orders that TQMC, Mr. Mathiesen,
Taylor Mathiesen and Mr. Sam be found guilty of civil contempt for
breaching the Document Production Order, and lump-sum and ongoing fines against
those parties.

[
54
]

The Document Production Order required TQMC to disclose:

a)

“any and all documents related to determining the proper amounts
according to the Sub-lease between the parties dated March 14, 2005,
specifically in relation to the common area expenses” (“Order 1”);

b)

“a copy of the lease…dated June 23, 2004 between the British
Columbia Ferry Services Inc. and Tsawwassen Quay Market Corporation…” (“Order 2”);
and

c)

“measurements of the common areas of the Tsawwassen Market, from
2005 to 2010” (“Order 3”).

[
55
]

As set out earlier in these reasons, a finding of civil contempt
requires this Court to conclude that the order in question clearly and
unequivocally sets out what should or should not be done; that the party
alleged to have breached the order had actual knowledge of the order; and that
the party that is alleged to have breached the order must have intentionally done
the act that the order prohibited.

Analysis – Alleged Breach of Order
1

[
56
]

The application for contempt of Order 1 must fail. I find that the
Document Production Order does not unequivocally state what should be done.

[
57
]

The Court in
R (Mark Dean Harris) v. The
Official Solicitor to the Supreme Court
, [2001] EWHC 798 Admin (Eng. Q.B.)
at para. 68 provides relevant principles for determining whether the elements
for contempt are met:

(i)         No order will be enforced by
committal unless it is expressed in clear, certain and unambiguous language. So
far as this is possible, the person affected should know with complete
precision what it is that he is required to do or to abstain from doing.

…

(iii)       An
order should not require the person to whom it is addressed to cross-refer to
other material in order to ascertain his precise obligation. Looking only at
the order the party enjoined must be able to find out from the four walls of it
exactly what it is that he must not do.

[
58
]

The requirement to produce “any and all” documents related to
determining the proper amounts for common area expenses payable under the
Sublease is so overly broad that the level of disclosure required is unclear. That
is, is it necessary to produce back-up documents such as invoices for various expenses
as well as proof of payment of such expenses such as cancelled cheques or bank
statements or simply internal accounting records setting out how common area
expenses were calculated? The order for production of documents is, in my view,
ambiguous.

[
59
]

As well, Order 1 requires TQMC to produce documents concerning the ”proper
amounts owing” under the Sublease. Proper amounts owing is certainly a matter
of opinion, to be decided by a trier of fact. In addition, the cross-reference
to the Sublease in the order requires the party subject to the order to review
the Sublease to determine what common area expenses are at issue.

[
60
]

The Disclosure Order also does not set out whether the documents to
be produced are only those within TQMC’s power, possession or control or
whether TQMC was required to produce documents in the possession of third
parties, such as BC Ferries, which are not under their control. This raises
additional ambiguity.

[
61
]

Given my finding that Order 1 is not clear and unequivocal it is not
necessary for me to consider the other elements required to be proven in an
application for a civil contempt order.

Analysis – Alleged Breach of Order
2

[
62
]

Order 2 requires disclosure of the lease dated June 23, 2004 between
British Columbia Ferry Services Inc. and TQMC. The parties accept that this is
a reference to the head lease between TQMC and BC Ferries for the Tsawwassen
Market.

[
63
]

Order 2 does not stipulate whether TQMC is required to disclose only
the copy of the head lease in its possession or whether it is required to
obtain a copy of the head lease from British Columbia Ferry Services Inc. Further,
the order provides no deadline for disclosure (and I note that the same applies
to Order 1 and Order 3). Arguably, TQMC cannot be found in breach of the order
as there is no stipulation as to when the lease is required to be produced. For
these reasons, Order 2 is ambiguous.

[
64
]

In addition, even if I was to have found that TQMC was only required
by Order 2 to produce the head lease in its possession, I am not satisfied
beyond a reasonable doubt that they have failed to do so or that they have intentionally
failed to do so. In a civil contempt application, the onus is on the applicant
to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the respondent has failed to comply
with an order and did so intentionally.

[
65
]

Mr. Mathiesen has sworn an affidavit which
includes a copy of correspondence sent from his then counsel to counsel for
Delane, Mr. O’nions, dated November 8, 2021, enclosing a copy of the head lease
dated June 24, 2004. In correspondence dated November 18, 2021 Mr. O’nions
wrote to TQMC’s counsel taking the position that TQMC had failed to provide the
complete head lease as pages were missing and the document provided had not
been signed.

[
66
]

There is insufficient evidence on which I can find that the head
lease provided by TQMC on November 8, 2021 was not the only such document in
their possession or control – and therefore there is insufficient evidence on
which I can find that TQMC intentionally breached Order 2.

Analysis – Alleged Breach of Order
3

[
67
]

Order 3 requires TQMC to “disclose measurements of the common areas
of the Tsawwassen Market, from 2005 to 2010”.

[
68
]

This order does not stipulate whether TQMC is to produce documents
which show the measurements of Tsawwassen Market’s common areas during each of
the years from and between 2005 and 2010 or to somehow provide measurements of
those areas during this period by, for example, reviewing drawings of the
market and calculating the size of the common areas. As a result, I find that
Order 3 is ambiguous.

[
69
]

Further, I am not satisfied that Delane has proven beyond a
reasonable doubt that TQMC has failed to provide this information and did so
intentionally. TQMC’s evidence, set out in Mr. Mathiesen’s affidavit, is
that his then counsel wrote to counsel for Delane on November 8, 2021 and
advised that “there are no documents which show the measurements of the actual
common areas”. This is the only evidence I have with respect to the
availability of such documents – which is simply that they do not exist.

[
70
]

There is insufficient evidence on which I can find beyond a
reasonable doubt that TQMC intentionally failed to produce documents showing
measurements of the common areas of the Tsawwassen Market in breach of Order 3.

Conclusion – Application No. 3

[
71
]

In summary, I do not find that the Document Disclosure Order was
unequivocal in respect of Orders 1, 2 and 3, which militates against a finding
of civil contempt. In addition, I am unable to find that Delane has proven
beyond a reasonable doubt that Taylor Mathiesen had knowledge of each of these
orders. His evidence is that he had no knowledge of the order and had no role
in document disclosure. Finally, I am unable to find beyond a reasonable doubt
that TQMC, Mr. Mathiesen, Mr. Sam or Taylor Mathiesen intentionally
breached the Document Disclosure Order.

[
72
]

For these reasons Application No. 3 is dismissed.

[
73
]

TQMC seeks special costs of defending against this application,
relying upon decisions including
439288 B.C. Ltd. v. Omineca Lama Ranch Inc.
,

2011 BCSC 865
and
Jampolsky v. Shattler
,

2010 BCSC 408
.

[
74
]

At para. 10 of
Omineca Lama
,

Justice
Watchuk stated that

[10]      Where
there is an alternative procedure, electing to apply first for a finding of
contempt is reprehensible in that it demonstrates an “unwarranted zeal and lack
of judgment” that is deserving of an order for special costs …

This case involved what Justice Watchuk found
was an unnecessary application for a finding of contempt against a court-appointed
receiver.

[
75
]

In
Jampolsky
,

Justice Greyell awarded special costs
against a party who brought an unnecessary application for contempt against
lawyers on the basis that they had committed a “dishonest or dishonourable act”:
at para. 18. Justice Greyell found that the contempt application brought
against lawyers acting against his client, amongst others, was reprehensible
and ordered special costs:
Jampolsky

at paras.
18-22
.

[
76
]

An order for special costs is discretionary. I am not satisfied that
the circumstances of this application are analogous to those in the
Omineca
Lama
or
Jampolsky
in that the application for contempt of the
Disclosure Order did not seek to impugn the reputation of TQMC or the personal
respondents. That is, I do not find that bringing this application for
contempt, notwithstanding that Delane had other options available to it to
compel document production under Rule 7-1, constitutes reprehensible conduct. Although
I find that the respondents are entitled to their costs, I decline to award
special costs.

Application No. 4

[
77
]

TQMC seeks an order that Delane pay security for costs of the Main Action
in amount of $15,000, failing which the action should be stayed. TQMC contends that
Delane’s financial circumstances suggest it will be unable to pay TQMC’s costs
should it be unsuccessful in their claim – which TQMC submits was commenced
over 10 years ago with little progress to date.

[
78
]

Section 236
of the
Business Corporations Act
, S.B.C. 2002, c.
57 [
BCA
], provides that the court may require a corporate plaintiff to
pay security for costs where it appears that the corporation may be unable to
pay the defendants costs if the defendant is successful.

[
79
]

In determining whether security for costs is appropriate the court
must balance the competing interests of not stifling a plaintiff’s legitimate
claim against the pressure imposed on a defendant responding to a claim by an
impecunious plaintiff:
Kropp v. Swaneset Bay Golf Course Ltd.
,
1997 CanLII 4037 (BC CA)
, 29 B.C.L.R.
(3d) 252 (C.A.) at para.
17
. The probability that a corporate plaintiff will be
deterred from pursuing a claim is not on its own a sufficient basis to decline
to order security for costs:
Kropp

at para.
17
.

[
80
]

Although orders under
s. 236
of the
BCA
are
discretionary once an applicant has shown that a corporate plaintiff will be unable
to pay costs should its claim fail, security will generally be ordered unless
the court is satisfied that there is no arguable defence to the claim:
Fat
Mel’s Restaurant Ltd. v. Canadian Northern Shield Insurance Co.
,

1993 CanLII 1669 (BC CA)
, 76
B.C.L.R. (2d) 231 (C.A.) at para.
16
.

[
81
]

The test for an application for security for costs in these
circumstances is summarized in
Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v.
Canadian Jewish Congress,
1999 CanLII 5860
(B.C.S.C.)

at para.
14
:

a)

Does it appear that the corporate plaintiff will be unable to pay
the defendant’s costs if the action fails?

b)

Has the plaintiff shown that it has exigible assets of sufficient
value to satisfy an award of costs?

c)

Does the defendant have an arguable defence?

d)

Would an order for costs visit undue hardship on the corporate
plaintiff such that it would prevent it from proceeding with its claim?

[
82
]

TQMC submits that the evidence establishes that Delane will likely be
unable to pay its costs if unsuccessful in the Main Action. In this respect
they point to, for example, Justice Adair’s reasons for judgment in
Delane
Industry Co. Ltd. v. Atkinson
(22 March, 2016), Vancouver Action No. S162131
(B.C.S.C.). In that case, which also arose after the termination of Delane’s
sublease at the Tsawwassen Market, Justice Adair found that Delane would
probably not be able to pay TQMC’s costs in that proceeding should it be
unsuccessful. Justice Adair ordered that Delane pay $14,000 in security for
each of two separate applications: see
Delane Industry Co. Ltd. v. Atkinson
,

2017 BCCA 79
at paras.
16-17
.

[
83
]

TQMC also refers to Mr. Au Yeung’s affidavit evidence filed in
this proceeding in which he deposed that Delane is impecunious, stating that
the company is “[s]pending so much money and law suits, now my companies are
almost broke and my children are grown up but they did not have very well
education because I spent so much of my time in law suites related to Garry
Mathiesen …”  and “I had sold one of our factories and spent all the money in
law suites. Now I can not afford to hire another lawyer, so I have to do it
myself now.”  In addition, TQMC says that Delane has not paid two costs awards previously
made against it, each in the amount of $500. Finally, TQMC submits that there
is no evidence that Delane owns real property and its corporate filings are not
up to date.

Analysis – Security for Costs

[
84
]

I am satisfied that it appears that Delane will be unable to pay a
costs award in favour of TQMC should it be unsuccessful in the Main Action. In
addition, Delane has not provided evidence that it has exigible assets of
sufficient value to satisfy an award of costs. Finally, I am satisfied that
TQMC has a meritorious defence to the claim advanced by Delane concerning
alleged overcharging for common area expenses. I need not say more on this
point and this comment should not be taken as suggesting that one side or the
other will ultimately prevail at trial.

[
85
]

What is at issue in this application is whether granting TQMC’s
order for costs will probably result in undue hardship such that Delane will be
unable to proceed with its claim. Delane has not lead evidence that an order
for security for costs would unfairly stifle its ability to pursue its claim
and result in an injustice.

[
86
]

I have considered Delane’s submission that Delane’s financial
hardship has been caused or contributed to by TQMC’s actions. I am not
satisfied that TQMC’s actions have resulted in Delane’s current financial
circumstances. The Sublease was terminated well over a decade ago. Prior to its
termination, Delane made the required rent payments to TQMC, including paying
for common area expenses. That money is spent. Although Delane’s current
difficult financial circumstances may have been caused in part by Mr. Au
Yeung’s pursuit of his various claims arising from the termination of the
Sublease, fault for this cannot be visited upon TQMC.

[
87
]

I have also considered TQMC’s failure to reimburse Delane for
“overstay” rent prior to finally abandoning its subleased premises at
Tsawwassen Market, which Justice Griffin found was payable. As TQMC points out,
Justice Griffin’s order requiring that it pay this amount is now over 10 years
old and no steps have been taken to renew this judgement.

[
88
]

I have also considered Delane’s submission that it would be unusual
or inappropriate to require security for costs in respect of what is
outstanding in the Main Action, being a reference to the Registrar to determine
the issue of appropriate common area expenses. Given Delane’s position that
additional documents are required, a further application will likely be
required concerning production of the documents it says are outstanding. In
addition, I expect that hearing before the Registrar will take at least two to
three days based on the nature of the dispute between the parties. As a result,
I do not consider that the security sought by TQMC is excessive.

[
89
]

In conclusion, I find that TQMC has satisfied the requirements for a
finding that Delane should provide security for costs in the amount of $15,000
in the Main Action. This security may be provided by way of cash deposit into
the trust account of Delane’s solicitors, or into the trust account of TQMC’s
solicitors if Delane is unrepresented in this action going forward. I order
that the Main Action is stayed until this security is provided.

[
90
]

TQMC is entitled to costs in respect of this application.

Remaining Costs Issues

[
91
]

TQMC seeks costs thrown away on a special costs basis in respect of
the applications brought by Delane dated February 3, 2022 and April 13, 2022, which
were abandoned at the hearing before me on July 11, 2022. In addition to costs
thrown away, TQMC, in my understanding, also seeks costs in respect of the
hearing before Justice Walker on May 16, 2022, at which he ordered that the
applications be heard at the same time as the parties’ dueling contempt
applications.

[
92
]

With respect to whether special costs are justified, TQMC submits
that the February 3 and April 13, 2022 applications include unfounded
allegations of fraud or other illegal conduct. Given that these applications
were prepared and filed by Mr. Au Yeung without the assistance of counsel
I do not consider that it would be appropriate to award special costs. TQMC is
entitled to its costs thrown away, including costs in respect of the
application heard by Justice Walker.

Conclusion

93
]

94
